title: Chromosomal Basis of Inheritance: Diploid Cells & Meiotic Gamete Formation
tagline: Homologous pairs in somatic cells, meiotic reduction division, and restoration of diploidy by fertilisation.
theoryHtml:
1. Chromosomes Carry Hereditary Units

Each cell of an organism contains long, thread-like structures called chromosomes in its nucleus, composed of DNA tightly coiled around histone proteins. Genes are organized in a linear sequence along these chromosomes. In sexually reproducing organisms, somatic (body) cells are diploid ($2n$), meaning chromosomes exist in matched homologous pairs—one inherited from the male parent and the other from the female parent.

2. Why Gametes Must Be Haploid ($n$)

If gametes (sperms and ova) were diploid like somatic cells, their fusion during fertilisation would double the chromosome count every single generation ($2n + 2n = 4n$, then $8n$, $16n$...), resulting in catastrophic biological chaos. To prevent this, specialized germ cells undergo meiosis (reduction division):

  • During meiosis, homologous chromosome pairs separate.
  • Each resulting gamete receives only one chromosome from each pair, making the gamete haploid ($n$).

3. Restoration of Diploidy by Fertilisation

When a haploid sperm cell ($n$) unites with a haploid ovum ($n$) during fertilisation (syngamy), the original species-specific diploid chromosome number ($n + n = 2n$) is precisely restored in the single-celled zygote, ensuring genomic stability across infinite generations.
pointsToRemember: Somatic body cells are diploid ($2n$) with chromosomes occurring in matched homologous pairs.
Meiosis halves the chromosome count to produce haploid ($n$) gametes carrying one set of genes.
Fertilisation unites haploid gametes ($n + n = 2n$) to restore species-specific diploidy in the zygote.
keyNotes: The parallel behaviour of Mendel's particulate factors and physical chromosomes during meiosis confirmed the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance formulated by Sutton and Boveri.

questions.question: How many pairs of chromosomes are normally present in the somatic (body) cells of a human being?
questions.explanation: Human diploid somatic cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes (46 chromosomes total: 22 pairs of autosomes + 1 pair of sex chromosomes).

questions.question: In a human cell, how many total chromosomes are present in a mature sperm cell or unfertilised ovum (gamete)?
questions.explanation: Human gametes are haploid (n = 23), containing 22 autosomes plus 1 sex chromosome (X or Y).

questions.question: What restores the normal diploid chromosome number (46 chromosomes) in the newly formed human zygote?
options: Fertilisation (Syngamy of haploid sperm n=23 and haploid ovum n=23)
questions.answer: Fertilisation (Syngamy of haploid sperm n=23 and haploid ovum n=23)
questions.explanation: Syngamy unites paternal haploid (n=23) and maternal haploid (n=23) pronuclei, restoring the somatic diploid (2n=46) state.

questions.question: How many types of genetically distinct gametes can be produced by a heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt)?
questions.explanation: According to the Law of Segregation, heterozygous Tt plants produce two equal classes of gametes: 50% with allele 'T' and 50% with allele 't'.

questions.question: How many types of genetically distinct gametes are produced by a dihybrid F1 pea plant with genotype RrYy?
options: 4 types (RY, Ry, rY, ry in 1:1:1:1 ratio)
questions.answer: 4 types (RY, Ry, rY, ry in 1:1:1:1 ratio)
questions.explanation: Due to independent assortment of R/r and Y/y, the dihybrid forms 4 types of gametes in equal 25% frequencies: RY, Ry, rY, and ry.

questions.question: How many total chromosomes are present in a normal human somatic (body) cell?
questions.explanation: Human somatic cells are diploid (2n) containing 46 chromosomes organized into 23 homologous pairs.

questions.question: How many chromosomes are carried by a normal, mature human ovum or sperm cell?
questions.explanation: Human gametes are haploid (n) formed via meiosis, containing exactly 23 unpaired chromosomes.

questions.question: What vital biological outcome is achieved by meiotic reduction division in the human life cycle?
options: It doubles the chromosome number in each generation
It halves the chromosome number in gametes to prevent doubling upon fertilisation
It converts all recessive genes into dominant ones
questions.answer: It halves the chromosome number in gametes to prevent doubling upon fertilisation
questions.explanation: Meiosis reduces chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n), so fertilisation restores the constant species diploid number.

questions.question: Who independently pointed out that the behaviour of chromosomes during meiosis parallels the behaviour of Mendel's factors?
questions.explanation: Sutton and Boveri (1902) formulated the Chromosomal Theory of Inheritance, uniting Mendelian genetics with cytology.

questions.question: A cell that possesses two complete sets of homologous chromosomes, one from each biological parent, is termed:
questions.explanation: Diploid (2n) cells possess two homologous sets of chromosomes, one contributed by the maternal parent and one by the paternal parent.

title: Environmental & Temperature-Dependent Sex Determination
tagline: Non-genetic sex determination in reptiles, snails, and temperature-dependent incubation of eggs.
theoryHtml:
1. Is Sex Always Genetically Determined?

In many animal species, sex is not dictated by chromosomes or genes at fertilisation. Instead, external environmental cues encountered during embryonic development or adulthood dictate whether an individual matures as a male or female.

2. Temperature-Dependent Sex Determination (TSD) in Reptiles

In several reptiles, the incubation temperature of the eggs during a critical thermosensitive period of embryonic development determines the sex of the hatchling:

  • Turtles (e.g., Green Sea Turtle): High incubation temperatures ($>31^\circ\text{C}$) yield predominantly female hatchlings, whereas lower incubation temperatures ($<28^\circ\text{C}$) produce predominantly male hatchlings ("Hot chicks and cool dudes").
  • Alligators & Crocodiles: The pattern is reversed or intermediate: higher temperatures ($32\text{--}34^\circ\text{C}$) typically produce males, while lower ($<31^\circ\text{C}$) or higher extreme temperatures yield females.

3. Snail Sex Plasticity (Crepidula & Land Snails)

In certain snails, such as marine slipper snails and some terrestrial gastropods, individuals can actually change their sex based on social contact, population density, or age. An individual may start life as a male and later transition into a female when settled alone, demonstrating that sex determination in these species is entirely non-genetic.
pointsToRemember: In many organisms, sex determination is environmental and non-genetic.
In reptiles (turtles, lizards, alligators), incubation temperature of eggs determines offspring sex.
Snails can change their sex during their adult lifetime, proving sex is not fixed by genes in all species.
keyNotes: Temperature-dependent sex determination poses significant conservation risks today; rising global temperatures due to climate change skew turtle populations overwhelmingly toward females.

questions.question: In which of the following organisms is the sex of the offspring determined by the temperature at which fertilised eggs are incubated?
questions.explanation: In many reptiles, such as turtles, alligators, and lizards, the incubation temperature of eggs during embryonic development determines hatchling sex.

questions.question: Which of the following animals can alter its sex during its lifetime, demonstrating that sex is not genetically fixed in all organisms?
questions.explanation: In certain snails (like slipper limpets), individuals can change their biological sex based on age and social environment.

questions.question: In green sea turtles, what is the phenotypic effect of incubating clutches of eggs at higher temperatures (>31°C)?
questions.explanation: In turtles, high incubation temperatures stimulate aromatase enzyme activity, producing overwhelmingly female hatchlings.

questions.question: What is the primary ecological threat posed by global warming to turtle populations exhibiting temperature-dependent sex determination?
options: Severe skewing of the sex ratio towards almost 100% females, leading to reproductive collapse
questions.answer: Severe skewing of the sex ratio towards almost 100% females, leading to reproductive collapse
questions.explanation: Rising nesting sand temperatures skew the population heavily toward females, resulting in an extreme scarcity of breeding males.

questions.question: In contrast to reptiles, human sex determination is:
options: Genetically determined at the exact moment of fertilisation by sex chromosomes
Determined by the mother's dietary calcium levels
questions.answer: Genetically determined at the exact moment of fertilisation by sex chromosomes
questions.explanation: In humans, sex is determined strictly by the chromosomal constitution of the sperm uniting with the egg at syngamy.

questions.question: What enzyme converts androgens into estrogens in temperature-dependent reptile embryos in response to heat?
questions.explanation: Aromatase converts testosterone into estradiol; its temperature-sensitive expression controls sexual differentiation in many reptiles.

questions.question: In American alligators, eggs incubated at intermediate temperatures around 32-34°C produce predominantly:
questions.explanation: In alligators, intermediate incubation temperatures (32-34°C) yield males, whereas lower or higher temperatures yield females.

questions.question: Which of the following organisms relies strictly on genetic sex chromosomes (XY or ZW) rather than environmental temperature?
questions.explanation: Humans rely strictly on the genetic XX-XY chromosomal mechanism, entirely unaffected by ambient environmental temperatures.

questions.question: In sequential hermaphroditic marine snails, an individual that starts life as a male and later becomes female is termed:
questions.explanation: Protandry refers to an animal maturing first as a male and subsequently transitioning into a female during its lifecycle.

questions.question: Can human parents influence the sex of their child by altering room temperature during gestation?
options: No, human sex is determined strictly genetically at fertilisation
Yes, but only during the third trimester
questions.answer: No, human sex is determined strictly genetically at fertilisation
questions.explanation: Human embryo sex is fixed at fertilisation by the sex chromosome (X or Y) delivered by the sperm; external temperature has zero effect.

title: Human Karyotype: Autosomes vs Sex Chromosomes (Allosomes)
tagline: 22 pairs of autosomes, 1 pair of allosomes, and structural dimorphism of X and Y chromosomes.
theoryHtml:
1. The Human Chromosome Complement

Every normal human somatic cell nucleus contains exactly 46 chromosomes organized into 23 pairs. These 23 pairs are classified into two distinct categories:

  • Autosomes (22 Pairs / 44 Chromosomes): Chromosomes numbered 1 through 22 that are identical in morphological structure in both biological males and females. Autosomes govern general somatic traits such as height, eye colour, skin pigmentation, and metabolic enzymes.
  • Sex Chromosomes / Allosomes (1 Pair / 2 Chromosomes): The 23rd pair that determines the biological sex of the individual.

2. The Allosomes: X and Y Chromosomes

The sex chromosomes exhibit marked structural and genetic dimorphism:

  • In Biological Females: The 23rd pair consists of two matched, large, metacentric chromosomes: $\mathbf{XX}$. Both chromosomes are identical in size and shape (homomorphic). A female's karyotype is represented as $44 + XX$.
  • In Biological Males: The 23rd pair is mismatched (heteromorphic) consisting of one normal-sized $\mathbf{X}$ chromosome and one distinctly smaller, truncated $\mathbf{Y}$ chromosome: $\mathbf{XY}$. A male's karyotype is represented as $44 + XY$.

3. The Role of the Y Chromosome

The human Y chromosome is physically much smaller than the X chromosome and contains fewer genes. However, it carries a master switch gene called the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region Y) that triggers the embryonic development of testes, initiating male sexual differentiation.
pointsToRemember: Human cells contain 23 pairs of chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes and 1 pair of sex chromosomes.
Biological females have two matching X chromosomes ($XX$); males have one X and one smaller Y ($XY$).
The SRY gene on the Y chromosome acts as the primary genetic switch directing male testis development.
keyNotes: The 22 pairs of autosomes are perfectly paired in both sexes; only the male sex chromosome pair ($XY$) is heteromorphic (mismatched in size).

questions.question: Out of the 23 chromosome pairs in human cells, how many pairs are autosomes (chromosomes that are perfectly matched and identical in males and females)?
questions.explanation: Humans have 22 pairs of autosomes controlling non-sex-linked somatic traits, identical in both sexes.

questions.question: What is the sex chromosome combination present in normal human biological females?
questions.explanation: Human females possess two homomorphic, normal-sized X sex chromosomes (44 + XX).

questions.question: What is the sex chromosome combination present in normal human biological males?
questions.explanation: Human males possess a heteromorphic mismatched pair consisting of one normal-sized X chromosome and one short Y chromosome (44 + XY).

questions.question: In human males, why does the Y chromosome appear distinctly smaller in size under a microscope compared to the X chromosome?
options: The Y chromosome is structurally shorter, containing fewer genes than the much larger X chromosome
questions.answer: The Y chromosome is structurally shorter, containing fewer genes than the much larger X chromosome
questions.explanation: The human Y chromosome is a smaller acrocentric chromosome with significantly fewer genes compared to the large submetacentric X chromosome.

questions.question: How many pairs of AUTOSOMES are present in a normal human diploid somatic cell?
questions.explanation: Out of the 23 pairs of chromosomes in human somatic cells, exactly 22 pairs are autosomes.

questions.question: What is the sex chromosome composition of a normal biological human male?
questions.explanation: Human males possess one X chromosome and one Y chromosome (XY) as their 23rd chromosomal pair.

questions.question: What is the sex chromosome composition of a normal biological human female?
questions.explanation: Human females possess two identical, homomorphic X chromosomes (XX) as their 23rd chromosomal pair.

questions.question: Why does the human Y chromosome appear distinctly smaller than the X chromosome under a microscope?
options: It contains significantly fewer genes and much less DNA content than the large X chromosome
It is made of RNA instead of DNA
It shrinks after every cell division
questions.answer: It contains significantly fewer genes and much less DNA content than the large X chromosome
questions.explanation: The Y chromosome has degenerated over evolutionary time, retaining only ~55-70 protein-coding genes compared to ~900-1000 genes on the X chromosome.

questions.question: Which master switch gene located on the human Y chromosome directs the undifferentiated gonads to develop into testes?
questions.explanation: The SRY (Sex-determining Region Y) gene on the Y chromosome encodes testis-determining factor, initiating male differentiation.

questions.question: What is the complete chromosomal notation for the karyotype of a normal human male somatic cell?
questions.explanation: A normal male karyotype has 44 autosomes plus one X and one Y chromosome (44 + XY = 46 chromosomes).

title: Mechanism of Human Sex Determination: Equal 50% Probability
tagline: Homogametic females, heterogametic males, and the 1:1 statistical sex ratio.
theoryHtml:
1. Gametogenesis in Females (Homogametic Sex)

Because a biological female has two matching $X$ chromosomes ($44 + XX$), all ova produced during oogenesis receive 22 autosomes and one $X$ chromosome ($22 + X$). Therefore, human females are homogametic—they produce only one kind of gamete regarding sex chromosomes.

2. Gametogenesis in Males (Heterogametic Sex)

A biological male has mismatched sex chromosomes ($44 + XY$). During spermatogenesis, homologous chromosomes segregate in meiosis, producing two distinct types of sperms in equal numbers ($50\%$ each):

  • 50% Gynosporms: Carry an $X$ chromosome ($22 + X$).
  • 50% Androsperms: Carry a $Y$ chromosome ($22 + Y$).

Hence, human males are heterogametic.

3. The Genetic Cross & Punnett Square

Sperm (Father) \ Ovum (Mother)$X$ ($100\%$)
$X$-bearing Sperm ($50\%$)$XX$ $\rightarrow$ Female child (Girl)
$Y$-bearing Sperm ($50\%$)$XY$ $\rightarrow$ Male child (Boy)

4. Equal 50% Statistical Probability

Because $X$-bearing and $Y$-bearing sperms are produced in equal numbers ($1:1$) and each has an equal chance of fertilising the ovum, every single pregnancy carries an exact $50\%$ probability ($1/2$) of being a boy and a $50\%$ probability ($1/2$) of being a girl, regardless of how many children a couple already has.
pointsToRemember: Females are homogametic ($XX$) and produce only $X$-bearing ova ($100\%$).
Males are heterogametic ($XY$) and produce $50\%$ $X$-bearing sperms and $50\%$ $Y$-bearing sperms.
The statistical probability of bearing a male or female child is strictly $1:1$ ($50\%$ each) at every conception.
keyNotes: Previous births have zero mathematical influence on the sex of future offspring; each conception is an independent 50% probability event.

questions.question: Which Mendelian principle states that alleles of two or more different gene pairs assort independently of one another during gamete formation?
questions.explanation: The Law of Independent Assortment states that factors (genes) for different traits segregate independently when gametes are formed.

questions.question: Which parent's gamete genetically determines the sex of the newborn child in human beings?
questions.explanation: All maternal ova carry an X chromosome. The father produces 50% X-bearing and 50% Y-bearing sperms; fertilization by a Y-sperm yields a boy, and by an X-sperm yields a girl.

questions.question: In an F2 dihybrid generation of 1600 pea plants derived from crossing RRYY × rryy, how many plants are expected to be 'Round Green' and 'Wrinkled Yellow', respectively?
options: 300 Round Green and 300 Wrinkled Yellow (3/16 of 1600 each)
questions.answer: 300 Round Green and 300 Wrinkled Yellow (3/16 of 1600 each)
questions.explanation: Expected frequencies: Round Green = 3/16 × 1600 = 300 plants; Wrinkled Yellow = 3/16 × 1600 = 300 plants.

questions.question: A plant with genotype Tt Rr is crossed with a plant of genotype tt rr (Dihybrid Testcross). What will be the resulting phenotypic ratio of the offspring?
options: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (25% Tall Round : 25% Tall Wrinkled : 25% Dwarf Round : 25% Dwarf Wrinkled)
questions.answer: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (25% Tall Round : 25% Tall Wrinkled : 25% Dwarf Round : 25% Dwarf Wrinkled)
questions.explanation: A dihybrid testcross (TtRr × ttrr) matches gamete proportions (1 TR : 1 Tr : 1 tR : 1 tr) directly with the tester's 'tr' gamete, producing a 1:1:1:1 phenotypic ratio.

questions.question: Why are human females called the 'homogametic sex'?
options: They produce two different kinds of eggs
All mature ova produced contain only one type of sex chromosome (an X chromosome)
questions.answer: All mature ova produced contain only one type of sex chromosome (an X chromosome)
questions.explanation: Because women have two X chromosomes (XX), all eggs produced through meiosis receive 22 autosomes + one X chromosome.

questions.question: What percentage of mature sperms produced by a healthy human male carry an X chromosome?
questions.explanation: Due to meiotic segregation of XY chromosomes, exactly 50% of sperms carry the X chromosome and 50% carry the Y chromosome.

questions.question: What is the biological sex of a child formed when an X-bearing ovum is fertilised by a Y-bearing sperm?
questions.explanation: Fertilisation of an X ovum by a Y sperm produces an XY zygote, which develops into a biological male child.

questions.question: What is the mathematical probability of a pregnant woman giving birth to a baby boy at any given pregnancy?
questions.explanation: Because X-bearing and Y-bearing sperms are produced in equal numbers, there is an exact 50% (1/2) chance of either sex.

questions.question: If a couple already has four biological daughters, what is the probability that their fifth child will be a son?
questions.explanation: Each conception is an independent random statistical event with an exact 50% probability of either sex.

questions.question: Which of the following genetic formulas correctly represents the chromosomal makeup of a human sperm cell?
questions.explanation: A haploid human sperm cell contains 22 autosomes plus either an X or a Y sex chromosome (22 + X or 22 + Y).

title: Paternal Determination of Offspring Sex & Debunking Social Stigma
tagline: Scientific evidence proving the father determines child sex, eradicating gender-based discrimination.
theoryHtml:
1. Biological Evidence: The Father Dictates Offspring Sex

In human reproduction, the biological sex of the child is entirely determined by which type of sperm from the father fertilises the mother's egg:

  • The mother can donate only an $X$ chromosome because her sex chromosome complement is exclusively $XX$.
  • The father produces two distinct populations of gametes: $50\%$ carry an $X$ chromosome and $50\%$ carry a $Y$ chromosome.
  • If an $X$-bearing sperm fertilises the egg $\rightarrow$ $X + X = XX$ ($\text{Female}$).
  • If a $Y$-bearing sperm fertilises the egg $\rightarrow$ $X + Y = XY$ ($\text{Male}$).

2. Debunking Social Stigma Against Women

In many patriarchal societies, women are unjustly blamed, harassed, and ostracized for giving birth to female children. Modern cytogenetics provides definitive scientific proof that:

  1. The mother has zero biological control over the sex of the child, as she contributes an identical $X$ chromosome in every single ovum.
  2. The genetic determinant of sex is strictly the paternal gamete (the sperm).
  3. Even from the father's perspective, whether an $X$-sperm or $Y$-sperm reaches the egg first is an entirely random, natural statistical event governed by chance.

3. Legal Protections: Banning Pre-Natal Sex Determination

To eliminate sex-selective abortion (female foeticide) arising from this unscientific preference for sons, the Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act strictly criminalizes determining or disclosing the sex of a foetus using ultrasound or amniocentesis.
pointsToRemember: The father genetically determines the child's sex because only he produces $Y$-bearing sperms.
Women contribute an identical $X$ chromosome to every child and have zero role in determining sex.
Blaming mothers for bearing daughters is scientifically baseless; prenatal sex testing is illegal under the PCPNDT Act.
keyNotes: Science conclusively proves that the mother provides only an X chromosome; the father's sperm alone dictates whether the child develops into a boy (XY) or girl (XX).

questions.question: How many genetically distinct genotypes are produced in the F2 generation of a classic Mendelian dihybrid cross (RrYy self-pollinated)?
options: 9 genotypes (RRYY, RRYy, RRyy, RrYY, RrYy, Rryy, rrYY, rrYy, rryy)
questions.answer: 9 genotypes (RRYY, RRYy, RRyy, RrYY, RrYy, Rryy, rrYY, rrYy, rryy)
questions.explanation: A dihybrid cross produces 4 phenotypes (9:3:3:1) but exactly 3 × 3 = 9 distinct genotypes.

questions.question: If an unfertilised human ovum is accidentally fertilized by a sperm that lacks any sex chromosome (nullisomic, 22+0), what will be the sex chromosome constitution of the zygote?
questions.explanation: Maternal X (22+X) plus paternal nullisomy (22+0) yields 45,X0 monosomy (Turner syndrome).

questions.question: What is the genetic mechanism that guarantees an equal 50:50 genetic contribution of nuclear DNA from male and female parents to their child?
options: Meiotic reduction halves homologous chromosome pairs so each gamete carries exactly 23 maternal or paternal chromosomes, which fuse upon syngamy
Father donates all DNA; mother provides only cytoplasm
questions.answer: Meiotic reduction halves homologous chromosome pairs so each gamete carries exactly 23 maternal or paternal chromosomes, which fuse upon syngamy
questions.explanation: Biparental syngamy unites 23 paternal nuclear chromosomes with 23 maternal nuclear chromosomes to re-establish the 46-chromosome diploid genome.

questions.question: In dogs, if black coat colour (B) is dominant over brown coat colour (b), what cross should an investigator design to determine the dominance relationship and unknown genotype of a black dog?
options: Breed the black dog with another black dog only
Testcross the black dog with a pure-breeding brown dog (bb); if any brown puppies appear, the black dog is heterozygous (Bb); if all puppies are black, it is homozygous (BB)
questions.answer: Testcross the black dog with a pure-breeding brown dog (bb); if any brown puppies appear, the black dog is heterozygous (Bb); if all puppies are black, it is homozygous (BB)
questions.explanation: A testcross with the homozygous recessive brown mate (bb) unmasks whether the dominant black parent carries a hidden recessive allele 'b'.

questions.question: Which parent's gamete genetically determines whether the unborn child will be a boy or a girl?
questions.explanation: Because the mother only provides X chromosomes, the child's sex depends entirely on whether the father's fertilising sperm carries an X or a Y chromosome.

questions.question: Why is it scientifically absurd and unjust to blame a woman for giving birth to female children?
options: All eggs produced by the mother carry only X chromosomes, so she has zero influence over the sex of the child
Women produce more Y chromosomes than men
questions.answer: All eggs produced by the mother carry only X chromosomes, so she has zero influence over the sex of the child
questions.explanation: Mothers contribute only an X chromosome to all offspring; the paternal sperm alone determines whether the zygote becomes XX (female) or XY (male).

questions.question: Which Indian legislation prohibits sex-selection and pre-natal sex determination to combat female foeticide?
questions.explanation: The Pre-Conception and Pre-Natal Diagnostic Techniques (PCPNDT) Act strictly bans prenatal sex determination to prevent female foeticide.

questions.question: What is the primary motive behind the statutory ban on disclosing foetal sex via ultrasound scanning?
options: To prevent sex-selective female foeticide and maintain a healthy demographic gender balance
questions.answer: To prevent sex-selective female foeticide and maintain a healthy demographic gender balance
questions.explanation: Banning foetal sex disclosure prevents sex-selective abortions that cause an unnatural deficit of girls in the population.

questions.question: Can a human father pass his Y chromosome directly to his biological daughter?
options: Yes, 50% of daughters receive a Y chromosome
No, daughters inherit the father's X chromosome; only sons inherit the father's Y chromosome
Yes, if the mother has XX chromosomes
questions.answer: No, daughters inherit the father's X chromosome; only sons inherit the father's Y chromosome
questions.explanation: A father passes his X chromosome to all daughters (making them XX) and his Y chromosome to all sons (making them XY).

questions.question: In human fertilisation, what determines whether an X-bearing or Y-bearing sperm fertilises the ovum?
options: Pure statistical chance and random motility during sperm transit
The time of day coitus takes place
questions.answer: Pure statistical chance and random motility during sperm transit
questions.explanation: Fertilisation is a stochastic (random) biological process where both X and Y sperms have an equal opportunity to reach and penetrate the ovum.

title: Heredity & Evolution: Variations as Raw Material for Natural Selection
tagline: How heritable variations confer differential survival advantages in shifting ecological niches.
theoryHtml:
1. Connecting Heredity to Evolution

Evolution is the gradual, progressive change in the heritable characteristics of biological populations over successive generations. Heredity is the transmission engine of evolution: without heritable variation passed through germ-line DNA, evolution by natural selection could not occur.

2. The Beetle Population Case Study (Natural Selection)

Consider a population of red beetles living on green leafy bushes:

  • Predation Pressure: Crows see the red beetles easily against the green foliage and feed on them in large numbers.
  • Novel Variation: A rare mutation during reproduction produces a green beetle variant. This green trait is heritable and passed to its progeny.
  • Survival Advantage: Crows cannot easily spot the green beetles camouflaged against green leaves. While red beetles are eaten, green beetles survive, reproduce, and multiply.
  • Evolutionary Outcome: Over generations, the frequency of the green allele increases until the population evolves to become predominantly green—a classic illustration of natural selection acting on heritable variation.

3. Genetic Drift (Random Flukes)

Now consider a blue beetle variant arising in the same red population. Blue beetles are just as visible to crows as red beetles, conferring zero survival advantage. However, suppose an elephant stomps on the bush, randomly crushing most red beetles by sheer accident. By chance, the few surviving beetles happen to be blue. They reproduce, and the population becomes blue. This change in allele frequencies due to random chance rather than selection is called genetic drift.
pointsToRemember: Heritable variations in germ-cell DNA provide the raw material upon which natural selection operates.
Natural selection favours variations that confer adaptive survival advantages in a given ecological niche.
Genetic drift causes random fluctuations in allele frequencies in small populations due to chance events.
keyNotes: Natural selection directs evolution toward greater adaptation, whereas genetic drift causes random changes without necessarily promoting survival fitness.

questions.question: Why would Mendel's Law of Independent Assortment FAIL to hold true if two different gene loci were situated very close together on the SAME chromosome?
options: The genes would destroy each other
Closely linked genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together as a linkage group and do not assort independently into gametes
The plant would turn into a dwarf
questions.answer: Closely linked genes on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together as a linkage group and do not assort independently into gametes
questions.explanation: Genetic linkage occurs when syntenic genes are physically contiguous on the same chromosome, preventing independent meiotic segregation.

questions.question: If a human sperm carrying a Y chromosome fertilizes a mature ovum, why does the resulting zygote develop male gonads (testes) rather than ovaries?
options: The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region Y) which initiates testicular differentiation and testosterone secretion in early embryonic development
The mother's uterus turns into testes
questions.answer: The Y chromosome carries the SRY gene (Sex-determining Region Y) which initiates testicular differentiation and testosterone secretion in early embryonic development
questions.explanation: The master testis-determining factor SRY on the short arm of the Y chromosome triggers undifferentiated bipotential gonadal ridges to develop into testes.

questions.question: A cross between two heterozygous tall pea plants (Tt × Tt) yields 400 total offspring. Statistically, how many of these plants are expected to be PURE-BREEDING (homozygous)?
questions.explanation: Genotypic distribution: 1/4 TT (100) + 1/2 Tt (200) + 1/4 tt (100). Pure-breeding homozygotes are TT + tt = 100 + 100 = 200 plants (50%).

questions.question: What is the key advantage of sexual reproduction over asexual reproduction in driving evolution?
options: It creates rapid and extensive genetic variation by combining alleles from two parents, increasing adaptive survival capacity
questions.answer: It creates rapid and extensive genetic variation by combining alleles from two parents, increasing adaptive survival capacity
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction generates novel combinatorial genetic diversity via meiotic crossing over, independent assortment, and biparental syngamy.

questions.question: In the green bush beetle example, why did the green colour variation provide a decisive survival advantage?
options: Green beetles fly three times faster
Green colour camouflaged them against green leaves, protecting them from predatory crows
Green beetles were poisonous to crows
questions.answer: Green colour camouflaged them against green leaves, protecting them from predatory crows
questions.explanation: Camouflage against green foliage prevented crows from visually spotting green beetles, allowing them to survive and reproduce.

questions.question: The process whereby organisms better adapted to their environment tend to survive and produce more offspring is termed:
questions.explanation: Natural selection, formulated by Charles Darwin, is the mechanism of evolutionary change based on differential survival and reproduction.

questions.question: Random changes in the frequency of alleles in a small population caused by sheer accidental chance rather than adaptation are called:
questions.explanation: Genetic drift refers to random fluctuations in allele frequencies in a gene pool resulting from chance events (e.g., natural disasters).

questions.question: In which type of population does genetic drift produce the most pronounced evolutionary impact?
questions.explanation: Genetic drift exerts a dramatic effect in small populations where chance accidents can easily eliminate or fix rare alleles.

questions.question: Why is sexual reproduction advantageous over asexual reproduction in driving long-term evolutionary survival?
options: It constantly generates novel genetic combinations and variations to adapt to changing environments
It produces offspring twice as fast
questions.answer: It constantly generates novel genetic combinations and variations to adapt to changing environments
questions.explanation: Sexual reproduction recombines alleles, generating extensive genetic diversity essential for adapting to unpredictable ecological changes.

questions.question: If a beetle variation provides NO survival advantage (e.g., blue colour against green leaves), how can it still become dominant in a small population?
options: Through genetic drift caused by an accidental event that wipes out other variants
questions.answer: Through genetic drift caused by an accidental event that wipes out other variants
questions.explanation: By random chance (such as an elephant crushing most red beetles), the surviving blue beetles reproduce, establishing the trait via genetic drift.

title: Germ Plasm vs Somatoplasm: The Molecular Impossibility of Lamarckism
tagline: Weismann's barrier, germline DNA stability, and why starvation or mutilations are not inherited.
theoryHtml:
1. Jean-Baptiste Lamarck's Flawed Hypothesis

In the early 19th century, French biologist Jean-Baptiste Lamarck proposed the Theory of Inheritance of Acquired Characters. He hypothesized that physical changes acquired by an organism through the "use and disuse of organs" during its lifetime (e.g., a giraffe stretching its neck to reach high leaves) are directly transmitted to its offspring.

2. August Weismann's Germ Plasm Theory (1892)

German evolutionary biologist August Weismann dismantled Lamarckism by drawing a fundamental biological distinction between two cell lineages:

  • Somatoplasm (Somatic Cells): Cells forming all ordinary body tissues—muscles, bones, nerves, and skin. Somatic cells perform physiological body tasks but die with the individual.
  • Germ Plasm (Germ Cells / Gametes): Cells set aside early in embryogenesis dedicated exclusively to reproduction (sperms and ova). The germ plasm represents an unbroken immortal continuum across generations.

3. The Weismann Barrier

Genetic information flows strictly from the germline to somatic tissues during development, never in reverse. Somatic environmental modifications—such as severe starvation reducing body mass, amputation of a limb, or sun-tanned skin—alter only somatic proteins. Because there is no molecular mechanism for somatic changes to back-mutate the nucleotide sequence of germline DNA, acquired characters are never inherited.
pointsToRemember: Lamarck hypothesized inheritance of acquired traits through use and disuse; Weismann disproved this experimentally.
Weismann's Germ Plasm Theory: Genetic info resides in germ cells and is segregated from somatic body cells.
The 'Weismann Barrier' prevents somatic cellular changes from altering nucleotide sequences in gametes.
keyNotes: Only mutations that occur in the DNA of germ cells (sperms and ova) can be transmitted to subsequent generations.

questions.question: Why do changes in non-reproductive somatic body tissues (such as weight loss during starvation) fail to be passed on to future generations?
options: Somatic tissue changes do not alter the nucleotide sequence of DNA in the germ cells (sperms and ova)
Only female parents pass on traits
questions.answer: Somatic tissue changes do not alter the nucleotide sequence of DNA in the germ cells (sperms and ova)
questions.explanation: Only genetic changes occurring in germline DNA of gametogenic cells are transmitted across generations.

questions.question: Why does a woman who suffers from severe malnutrition during pregnancy give birth to an infant with low birth weight, but the infant's own biological children have normal birth weight when properly nourished?
options: Low birth weight is a dominant mutation
Maternal undernutrition causes an acquired phenotypic change in somatic tissue that does not alter germline DNA sequences, so it is not inherited by the next generation
Children inherit traits only from grandparents
questions.answer: Maternal undernutrition causes an acquired phenotypic change in somatic tissue that does not alter germline DNA sequences, so it is not inherited by the next generation
questions.explanation: Nutritional deficits affect somatic fetal intrauterine growth without changing gametogenic nucleotide sequences, so offspring with adequate nutrition attain normal weight.

questions.question: In human genetics, why is a father UNABLE to pass an X-linked recessive genetic disorder (such as red-green colour blindness or hemophilia) directly to his son?
options: A father always contributes his Y chromosome to his biological son; the son inherits his single X chromosome exclusively from his mother
questions.answer: A father always contributes his Y chromosome to his biological son; the son inherits his single X chromosome exclusively from his mother
questions.explanation: A male child receives his Y chromosome from his father and his X chromosome from his mother; thus, paternal X-linked alleles pass only to daughters.

questions.question: A child has blood group O. If the mother has blood group B, which of the following CANNOT possibly be the blood group of the biological father?
questions.explanation: A child with group O (ii) must inherit one 'i' allele from each parent. A man with group AB (IA IB) possesses no 'i' allele and cannot father a group O child.

questions.question: Who proposed the 'Theory of Inheritance of Acquired Characters' that was later refuted by modern genetics?
questions.explanation: Lamarck proposed that traits acquired through use and disuse during an organism's lifetime could be inherited by its offspring.

questions.question: Why does a beetle population starved due to plant disease experience reduced body weight that is NOT passed to future well-fed generations?
options: Starvation alters the beetle's exoskeleton colour
Weight loss is a somatic phenotypic response to nutrient scarcity, leaving germ-cell DNA unaltered
questions.answer: Weight loss is a somatic phenotypic response to nutrient scarcity, leaving germ-cell DNA unaltered
questions.explanation: Under-nutrition reduces somatic body tissue mass without altering the genetic nucleotide sequences inside gametes.

questions.question: What is the principle known as the 'Weismann Barrier'?
options: The strict unidirectional flow of genetic information from germ cells to somatic cells, preventing somatic feedback into gametes
A physical wall between testes and ovaries
questions.answer: The strict unidirectional flow of genetic information from germ cells to somatic cells, preventing somatic feedback into gametes
questions.explanation: The Weismann barrier asserts that changes occurring in somatic tissues cannot feed back to alter the hereditary germ-line DNA.

questions.question: Which of the following alterations CAN be inherited by biological offspring?
options: A gene mutation in a spermatogonium cell inside the testis
A scar resulting from a burn on the forearm
Fluency in speaking three foreign languages
Muscle hypertrophy from daily gym workouts
questions.answer: A gene mutation in a spermatogonium cell inside the testis
questions.explanation: Spermatogonia are germ cells; a mutation in their DNA is carried by mature sperms and transmitted to offspring.

questions.question: If a woman pierces her ears for earrings, why are her daughters not born with pierced earlobes?
options: Ear piercing only alters cartilage in somatic tissue without affecting reproductive gamete DNA
Ear piercing is dominant only in males
The piercing heals inside the uterus
Daughters inherit traits only from fathers
questions.answer: Ear piercing only alters cartilage in somatic tissue without affecting reproductive gamete DNA
questions.explanation: Piercing is an acquired somatic modification that has zero effect on the nucleotide sequence of germ-line chromosomes.

questions.question: Which of the following scientists conducted the famous 20-generation tail-docking experiment on mice?
questions.explanation: August Weismann amputated the tails of mice over 20 generations to decisively disprove Lamarck's theory of acquired inheritance.

title: Speciation Basics: Geographical Isolation & Genetic Divergence
tagline: How reproductive barriers, gene pool separation, and natural selection lead to the origin of new species.
theoryHtml:
1. What is Speciation?

A species is a population of reproducing organisms that can freely interbreed among themselves under natural conditions to produce fertile offspring. Speciation is the evolutionary process by which an existing ancestral species splits into two or more genetically distinct, reproductively isolated descendant species.

2. Primary Drivers of Speciation

  • 1. Geographical Isolation (Allopatric Barrier): A physical geographical barrier—such as the emergence of a wide mountain range, a major river widening, or continental drift—subdivides a continuous population into isolated sub-populations. Gene flow between these groups drops to zero.
  • 2. Genetic Drift: In each separated sub-population, random chance events alter allele frequencies independently over generations.
  • 3. Differing Natural Selection Pressures: Each isolated sub-population encounters distinct ecological challenges—different predators, ambient temperatures, vegetation, and food sources. Natural selection favours different adaptive variations in each group.

3. Reproductive Isolation (The Final Threshold)

Over thousands of generations, accumulated genetic differences in DNA, chromosome structure, mating rituals, and gamete biochemistry become so profound that even if the geographical barrier disappears, individuals from the two groups can no longer interbreed to produce fertile offspring. At this point, speciation is complete.
pointsToRemember: A species is a group of interbreeding individuals capable of producing fertile offspring.
Speciation occurs through geographical isolation, independent genetic drift, and differing natural selection.
Reproductive isolation marks the permanent emergence of a new species when interbreeding is no longer possible.
keyNotes: Geographical isolation can lead to speciation only in sexually reproducing organisms; it does not drive speciation in strictly self-pollinating or asexually dividing species.

questions.question: In garden peas, yellow cotyledon colour (Y) is dominant over green cotyledon colour (y), and round seed shape (R) is dominant over wrinkled shape (r). What is the phenotype of a plant with genotype Rr yy?
questions.explanation: Genotype 'Rr' produces the dominant Round shape, while 'yy' produces the homozygous recessive Green colour.

questions.question: What is the expected phenotypic ratio when a plant with genotype Rr Yy is testcrossed with rr yy?
options: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (Round Yellow : Round Green : Wrinkled Yellow : Wrinkled Green)
questions.answer: 1 : 1 : 1 : 1 (Round Yellow : Round Green : Wrinkled Yellow : Wrinkled Green)
questions.explanation: A dihybrid testcross (RrYy × rryy) yields 1 Round Yellow : 1 Round Green : 1 Wrinkled Yellow : 1 Wrinkled Green (1:1:1:1).

questions.question: Which of the following cellular processes ensures that every daughter cell produced by binary fission in bacteria receives an exact copy of the parent's genetic material?
questions.explanation: Bacterial chromosome duplication relies on semi-conservative DNA replication prior to binary fission.

questions.question: What is the biological definition of a species?
options: A group of organisms that look identical under an optical microscope
A group of naturally interbreeding organisms capable of producing viable, fertile offspring
All organisms living in the same geographical forest
Organisms that consume the exact same food source
questions.answer: A group of naturally interbreeding organisms capable of producing viable, fertile offspring
questions.explanation: A biological species consists of organisms capable of interbreeding in nature to produce fertile, viable offspring.

questions.question: Which of the following physical barriers can cause geographical isolation between sub-populations?
options: Formation of a wide mountain range or new river channel
A drop in atmospheric oxygen by 0.1%
questions.answer: Formation of a wide mountain range or new river channel
questions.explanation: Physical geographical barriers like rivers, oceans, or mountain ranges split populations and prevent gene flow.

questions.question: Why does geographical isolation NOT cause speciation in strictly asexually reproducing organisms like bacteria?
options: Bacteria do not have cell membranes
Bacteria reproduce by binary fission without interbreeding, so reproductive isolation has no functional meaning
questions.answer: Bacteria reproduce by binary fission without interbreeding, so reproductive isolation has no functional meaning
questions.explanation: Speciation via geographical isolation relies on stopping sexual gene flow between interbreeding populations.

questions.question: At what definitive point can two diverging populations be declared two separate species?
options: When they develop different body colours
When they are permanently unable to interbreed and produce fertile offspring upon contact
When their life expectancy differs by 1 year
questions.answer: When they are permanently unable to interbreed and produce fertile offspring upon contact
questions.explanation: Reproductive isolation—the inability to interbreed and generate fertile offspring—is the definitive criterion for distinct species.

questions.question: What term describes the exchange of genes between different interbreeding populations of the same species?
questions.explanation: Gene flow is the transfer of genetic material between populations through migration and interbreeding.

questions.question: What role does natural selection play in speciation among geographically isolated populations?
options: It preserves identical traits in both groups
It selects different adaptive variations suited to each sub-population's unique local environment
It accelerates the return of the geographical barrier
It forces all organisms to stop mating
questions.answer: It selects different adaptive variations suited to each sub-population's unique local environment
questions.explanation: Different local habitats present different selective pressures, steering isolated gene pools along divergent evolutionary paths.

questions.question: Which of the following is a classic pre-zygotic reproductive isolating mechanism?
options: Different mating seasons or courtship behaviours
questions.answer: Different mating seasons or courtship behaviours
questions.explanation: Behavioural differences in courtship songs or incompatible breeding seasons prevent mating, maintaining reproductive isolation.

title: ABO Blood Group Inheritance: Multiple Alleles & Co-dominance
tagline: The three alleles I^A, I^B, and i; co-dominance in AB blood, and inheritance problem-solving.
theoryHtml:
1. The ABO Blood Group System

In human beings, the ABO blood group is controlled by a single gene: the $I$ gene (isoagglutinogen) located on chromosome 9. This gene governs the production of glycoprotein antigens protruding from the plasma membrane of red blood cells (erythrocytes).

2. Multiple Alleles

Unlike classic Mendelian traits that feature only two alleles, the human $I$ gene exists in three alternative allelic forms (multiple allelism):

  • $\mathbf{I^A}$: Produces antigen A on red blood cells (Dominant over $i$).
  • $\mathbf{I^B}$: Produces antigen B on red blood cells (Dominant over $i$).
  • $\mathbf{i}$: Produces no surface antigen (Recessive allele).

Because every individual is diploid, each person can carry at most any two of these three alleles.

3. Co-dominance in Blood Group AB

When both dominant alleles $\mathbf{I^A}$ and $\mathbf{I^B}$ are present together in an individual ($\mathbf{I^A I^B}$), neither allele masks the other. Instead, both express fully and simultaneously, producing both antigen A and antigen B on erythrocytes. This phenomenon is called co-dominance.

4. Genotypes and Phenotypes

Blood Group (Phenotype)Possible Genotype(s)Antigens on RBCs
Type A$I^A I^A$ or $I^A i$Antigen A
Type B$I^B I^B$ or $I^B i$Antigen B
Type AB$I^A I^B$ (Co-dominant)Both Antigen A & B
Type O$ii$ (Homozygous recessive)Neither Antigen
pointsToRemember: Human ABO blood groups are controlled by the gene $I$ which has three alleles: $I^A$, $I^B$, and $i$.
Alleles $I^A$ and $I^B$ are completely dominant over recessive $i$.
Alleles $I^A$ and $I^B$ are co-dominant with each other, producing blood group AB in heterozygous $I^A I^B$ individuals.
keyNotes: A child with blood group O ($ii$) born to a mother with blood group A must mean the mother's genotype is heterozygous $I^A i$ and the father must carry at least one recessive $i$ allele.

questions.question: A man with blood group A marries a woman with blood group O, and their daughter has blood group O. What are the genotypes of the father and mother?
options: Father: IA i (Heterozygous); Mother: ii (Homozygous recessive)
questions.answer: Father: IA i (Heterozygous); Mother: ii (Homozygous recessive)
questions.explanation: Blood group O requires the homozygous recessive genotype 'ii'. The daughter inherits one 'i' from the mother (ii) and must inherit the second 'i' from the father, proving the father is heterozygous IA i.

questions.question: Which of the following blood group alleles in the human ABO system are co-dominant to each other, and dominant over allele 'i'?
questions.explanation: Alleles IA and IB are codominant (producing blood group AB in IA IB individuals) and both are completely dominant over recessive allele i.

questions.question: If a homozygous tall plant (TT) is crossed with a heterozygous tall plant (Tt), what percentage of the progeny will be PHENOTYPICALLY TALL?
questions.explanation: TT × Tt yields 50% TT and 50% Tt; all 100% of the offspring exhibit the dominant tall phenotype.

questions.question: Why do identical (monozygotic) human twins share exactly identical genotypes and phenotypic traits at birth, while fraternal (dizygotic) twins do NOT?
options: Identical twins develop from a single fertilized zygote that splits into two embryos, sharing 100% identical DNA; fraternal twins arise from two separate eggs fertilized by two different sperms
Fraternal twins develop outside the mother
questions.answer: Identical twins develop from a single fertilized zygote that splits into two embryos, sharing 100% identical DNA; fraternal twins arise from two separate eggs fertilized by two different sperms
questions.explanation: Monozygotic twins originate from cleavage of a single zygote (identical genomes); dizygotic twins originate from two separate ovulations/fertilizations (share ~50% alleles like siblings).

questions.question: How many total distinct alleles control the ABO blood group system in the human population?
questions.explanation: The human ABO blood group system is governed by three multiple alleles: I^A, I^B, and i.

questions.question: What genetic phenomenon is illustrated when an individual with genotype I^A I^B exhibits both A and B antigens equally?
questions.explanation: In co-dominance, both alleles express their phenotypic effects simultaneously and fully in the heterozygote.

questions.question: What is the only possible genotype of an individual possessing blood group O?
questions.explanation: Blood group O is homozygous recessive, requiring two copies of the 'i' allele (ii).

questions.question: A man with blood group A marries a woman with blood group B. Their first child has blood group O. What are the genotypes of the parents?
options: Father: I^A I^A; Mother: I^B I^B
Father: I^A i; Mother: I^B i
questions.answer: Father: I^A i; Mother: I^B i
questions.explanation: For a child to have blood group O (ii), each parent must donate a recessive 'i' allele, meaning both must be heterozygous (I^A i and I^B i).

questions.question: How many possible genotypes and how many possible phenotypes exist in the human ABO blood group system?
questions.explanation: The 6 genotypes (I^A I^A, I^A i, I^B I^B, I^B i, I^A I^B, ii) produce 4 phenotypes (A, B, AB, O).

questions.question: Can two parents with blood group O (ii) ever have a biological child with blood group A or B?
options: No, because blood group O parents carry only recessive 'i' alleles and lack the I^A or I^B alleles
Yes, if the child is male
questions.answer: No, because blood group O parents carry only recessive 'i' alleles and lack the I^A or I^B alleles
questions.explanation: Two 'ii' parents can produce only 'i'-bearing gametes, so all their biological offspring must have blood group O (ii).

title: Comprehensive Genetics Problem Solving: Ratios, Crosses & Pedigree Logic
tagline: Mastery problem-solving for monohybrid, dihybrid, test cross, and human genetic pedigrees.
theoryHtml:
1. Genetic Cross Problem-Solving Protocol

To deterministically solve any Mendelian genetics numerical or conceptual problem:

  1. Identify Alleles: Assign uppercase letters to dominant alleles ($T, R, Y$) and corresponding lowercase letters to recessive alleles ($t, r, y$).
  2. Deduce Parental Genotypes: Use phenotypic clues. If a parent displays the recessive phenotype, its genotype is always homozygous recessive (e.g., $tt$, $rr$). If a parent displays a dominant trait but has a recessive offspring, that parent must be heterozygous (e.g., $Tt$).
  3. Determine Gametes: Segregate alleles cleanly into haploid gametes ($T$ and $t$, or $RY, Ry, rY, ry$).
  4. Construct the Punnett Grid: Cross all possible male and female gametes to calculate genotypic and phenotypic probabilities.

2. The Test Cross (Mendel's Diagnostic Tool)

How can you determine whether a tall pea plant is homozygous dominant ($TT$) or heterozygous ($Tt$)? You perform a test cross by breeding the individual of unknown genotype with a homozygous recessive ($tt$) individual:

  • If the unknown is homozygous ($TT \times tt$): $100\%$ of progeny are tall ($Tt$).
  • If the unknown is heterozygous ($Tt \times tt$): Progeny segregate into $\mathbf{1\text{ Tall} : 1\text{ Dwarf}}$ ($50\% : 50\%$). The appearance of even a single dwarf plant proves the tall parent was heterozygous!

3. Summary of Standard Mendelian Ratios

  • Monohybrid $F_2$ Phenotypic Ratio: $3 : 1$
  • Monohybrid $F_2$ Genotypic Ratio: $1 : 2 : 1$ ($1\,TT : 2\,Tt : 1\,tt$)
  • Monohybrid Test Cross Ratio: $1 : 1$ ($1\,Tt : 1\,tt$)
  • Dihybrid $F_2$ Phenotypic Ratio: $9 : 3 : 3 : 1$
  • Dihybrid Test Cross Ratio: $1 : 1 : 1 : 1$
pointsToRemember: A test cross breeds an individual with unknown dominant phenotype against a homozygous recessive ($tt$) tester.
A $1:1$ test cross ratio proves the dominant parent is heterozygous ($Tt$); a $100\%$ dominant result proves homozygosity ($TT$).
Mastery of Mendelian ratios ($3:1$, $1:2:1$, $9:3:3:1$, $1:1$, $1:1:1:1$) enables rapid analysis of complex genetic crosses.
keyNotes: In all genetic calculations, probabilities multiply for independent events (Rule of Multiplication: $1/2 	imes 1/2 = 1/4$) and add for mutually exclusive alternatives (Rule of Addition: $1/4 + 1/4 = 1/2$).

questions.question: Which of the following represents a reciprocal cross for the parental cross: Female Tall (TT) × Male Dwarf (tt)?
questions.explanation: A reciprocal cross reverses the sexes associated with each parental phenotype (Female Dwarf tt × Male Tall TT).

questions.question: How many total autosomes are present in a normal human UNFERTILISED OVUM?
questions.explanation: A mature secondary oocyte/ovum contains 22 autosomes plus 1 X sex chromosome (total 23 chromosomes).

questions.question: In an F2 dihybrid cross (RrYy selfed), what is the probability of obtaining an offspring that is HOMOZYGOUS for BOTH dominant traits (RRYY)?
questions.explanation: The double homozygous dominant genotype RRYY appears in only 1 out of 16 squares in the dihybrid Punnett table (probability = 1/16).

questions.question: In a trihybrid self-cross between two individuals of genotype Tt Rr Yy, what is the probability of obtaining an offspring that is HOMOZYGOUS RECESSIVE for ALL THREE traits (tt rr yy)?
questions.explanation: For independent unlinked genes: P(tt) = 1/4, P(rr) = 1/4, P(yy) = 1/4. P(tt rr yy) = 1/4 × 1/4 × 1/4 = 1/64.

questions.question: A man with blood group A and a woman with blood group B have a child with blood group O. What is the probability that their NEXT child will have blood group AB?
questions.explanation: Having a group O child (ii) proves parents are IA i and IB i. Cross IA i × IB i produces: 1/4 IA IB (AB), 1/4 IA i (A), 1/4 IB i (B), 1/4 ii (O). Probability of AB = 25%.

questions.question: In an experimental pedigree analysis, two normal parents have a child with an autosomal recessive metabolic disorder (Phenylketonuria / PKU). What is the probability that their next healthy, unaffected child is a CARRIER (heterozygous) of the mutant PKU allele?
questions.explanation: Both parents are carriers (Pp × Pp). Among unaffected offspring (PP, Pp, Pp), 2 out of 3 (2/3) are heterozygous carriers (Pp).

questions.question: A plant heterozygous for three independent genes (Aa Bb Cc) is testcrossed with an individual of genotype aa bb cc. How many distinct phenotypic classes will appear in the progeny, and in what ratio?
questions.explanation: A trihybrid testcross (AaBbCc × aabbcc) generates 2³ = 8 distinct phenotypic classes in equal 1:1:1:1:1:1:1:1 proportions.

questions.question: Why does the presence of a single functional dominant allele 'T' in a heterozygous pea plant (Tt) result in the SAME full tall height as a homozygous dominant plant (TT)?
options: The recessive allele is physically deleted
The single 'T' allele produces sufficient functional gibberellin-biosynthesizing enzyme above the critical physiological threshold required for maximal stem cell elongation
Dwarf genes turn into tall genes
questions.answer: The single 'T' allele produces sufficient functional gibberellin-biosynthesizing enzyme above the critical physiological threshold required for maximal stem cell elongation
questions.explanation: Enzymatic haplosufficiency: one functional 'T' allele synthesizes adequate active enzyme to generate normal gibberellin levels, achieving full wild-type stem elongation.

questions.question: Consider a population of 1000 pea plants in an F2 monohybrid generation exhibiting 750 tall and 250 dwarf plants. If ALL the 750 tall plants are individually self-pollinated, what will be the total proportion of dwarf plants in the resulting F3 generation?
questions.explanation: The 750 tall plants comprise 250 TT (1/3) and 500 Tt (2/3). TT selfing yields 0 dwarf; 2/3 Tt selfing yields 1/4 dwarf offspring. Total F3 dwarf proportion = 2/3 × 1/4 = 2/12 = 1/6 (16.67%).

questions.question: What is the expected phenotypic ratio in the progeny of a test cross involving a heterozygous tall pea plant (Tt x tt)?
questions.explanation: Crossing Tt with tt produces 50% Tt (Tall) and 50% tt (Dwarf), giving the classic 1:1 test cross ratio.
